q: Does an open-source Geant4-DNA reimplementation of the paper's geometry + physics + chemistry stages reproduce the 0.171 +/- 0.003 DSB/decay primitive for Cu-64 at 0.25 nm from the DNA axis, or is the number sensitive to TOPAS-nBio-specific chemistry parameters (OH lifetime, reaction radii, backbone volume definition)?
basis: The paper reports a headline MC primitive that we did not rerun. TOPAS-nBio is CC-BY-NC and gated; Geant4-DNA is fully open and shares the same physics/chemistry stack in principle but differs in default parameters, scoring hooks, and geometry primitives. The residual gap between the two implementations is the actual measure of MC-portability for this class of paper.
next_steps: Stand up a Geant4-DNA build (v11.2+ with G4EmDNAPhysics_option4 and G4EmDNAChemistry_option3), reconstruct the Zhu et al. 2020 fractal-chromatin geometry from published parameters, place Cu-64 point-sources at 0.25 nm and 1.15 nm on a randomly-chosen base pair, run G4RadioactiveDecay for 400k histories per point, score SSBs by the 0.13 OH-hit probability and 17.5 eV direct-hit threshold, and compare DSB/decay under an identical 10-bp opposite-strand rule. Report agreement or disagreement to 2 s.f.

q: How sensitive is the 47.1e-3 Bq/cell equi-lethal Cu-64 activity to the choice of biological-endpoint model (Humm-Charlton 1989 lethal-damage assumption vs. modern MEDRAS repair-kinetics, vs. LEM-IV local-effect, vs. PARTRAC-based cell-survival curves)?
basis: The paper anchors on Humm-Charlton Eq. 1, which assumes a fixed 194-DSB lethal threshold from a single 24-h cell cycle. Repair-competent models (MEDRAS, LEM-IV) predict very different equi-lethal activities for the same DSB yield because Auger-cluster damage is preferentially unrepairable. The paper mentions MEDRAS in passing but does not compute a MEDRAS endpoint.
next_steps: Wrap the paper's DSB primitives (Table 1) in three additional endpoint models: (a) MEDRAS with default fast/slow repair kinetics, (b) LEM-IV with published DNA-target parameters for CHO cells, (c) a Poisson-cluster damage-to-survival mapping from PARTRAC. Report each model's predicted equi-lethal activity for Cu-64 and compare the spread. A factor-of-2 spread would materially change any clinical dose-planning claim built on this paper.

q: Does the DSB yield per Cu-64 decay depend materially on the specific chemistry of the Cu-64-labeled targeting compound (Cu-DOTA, Cu-NOTA, Cu-ATSM, Cu-cyclam, antibody conjugates), and how does that dependence propagate to the equi-lethal activity for realistic clinical constructs?
basis: The paper models Cu-64 as a bare point source at 0.25 or 1.15 nm from the DNA axis. In practice Cu-64 is delivered as a chelate; the effective source-to-DNA distance distribution depends on nuclear uptake, chelate stability, and whether the construct intercalates, groove-binds, or stays in nucleoplasm. Table 1 shows a 10% swing between 0.25 nm and 1.15 nm; the full clinical range may be far wider.
next_steps: Compile published subcellular biodistribution data for Cu-64-ATSM, Cu-64-DOTA-TATE, and Cu-64-labeled antibody constructs (nuclear vs. cytoplasmic vs. membrane fractions from confocal or fractionation studies). Convolve those distributions with a distance-to-DNA kernel to produce a construct-specific effective DSB/decay. Compare the resulting equi-lethal activities to the paper's naked-Cu-64 number.

q: How sensitive is the reported 0.171 DSB/decay to the Auger-electron sub-keV spectrum used, given that ICRP-107, ENSDF, and the Livermore-Auger tables disagree by factors of order 2 on the softest Auger lines?
basis: The paper cites a Cu-64 electron yield of about 0.18 per decay; the ICRP-107 sum above 1 keV is about 0.228, and the total Auger sum is about 1.8. G4RadioactiveDecay's default database version was not specified in the paper's Methods. Sub-keV Auger electrons have ranges below 10 nm and can produce most of the DSBs.
next_steps: Rerun the (open-source) Geant4-DNA replica of the primitive under two Auger-spectrum choices: (i) G4RadioactiveDecay's ICRP-107 default, (ii) an explicit BrIccEmis-generated per-shell spectrum. Report the delta in DSB/decay. If the two disagree by more than 15%, flag the paper's number as spectrum-dependent and add a systematic error bar to Table 2.

q: Can an ML-driven fit over TOPAS-nBio simulation outputs across the panel of five radionuclides (125I, 123I, 111In, 99mTc, 64Cu) recover a compact, physically-interpretable RBE parameterization (LET-dependent alpha/beta or a track-structure-based effective-Q function) that predicts DSB/decay for a new Auger emitter without a fresh MC run?
basis: The paper produces 10 DSB/decay values (5 nuclides x 2 positions) at considerable compute cost. A surrogate model calibrated on those + a handful of monoenergetic-electron data points would let the community screen new therapy candidates cheaply. No such surrogate exists in the paper.
next_steps: Build a small (5-15 feature) dataset: per-nuclide LET spectrum moments, mean electron energy, Auger yield above 1 keV, source-to-axis distance, half-life. Target = DSB/decay from Table 1 (paper) or the reproduced primitives from Q1. Fit both a linear model and a gradient-boosted regressor with leave-one-nuclide-out cross-validation. Report LOO MAE and identify which features carry the signal. If LOO MAE is under 15%, publish the surrogate as a screening tool for Cu-67, Tb-161, Ac-225 daughters, etc.
